comments.text:
When computing the "average FPS" at any given resolution, it'd be better to normalize (i.e. express the FPS as percentages), before adding them together.
Otherwise, high FPS games will distort the average.

Let me illustrate this with a simple example:

Game 1: 
GPU 1: 50 FPS
GPU 2: 60 FPS

I.e. a 20% increase in FPS

Game 2:
GPU 1: 200 FPS
GPU 2: 300 FPS

I.e. a 50% increase in FPS.

Averaging:

Based on FPS:
GPU 1: 250 FPS
GPU 2: 360 FPS
Increase: 44% (current method)

Actual average increase:
(20% + 50%)/2 = 35%

This can also go the other way. However, from a statistical standpoint the "add all FPS and divide by number of games"-approach seems like bad style.
In your data set, you found the biggest difference in performance in a title with very high FPS (200+). Thus, most likely making the 3090 look better than it actually is.

Yes, at first I had to reduce settings to boost the frame rate at 4K, but shooters aren't about shadows and reflections... they are about winning.  The 60Hz refresh rate isn't that crippling, because the 43" size of my display compensates for the lower frame rate, I can see things that you simply cannot see on your PUNY 27" display.  It really has been my secret weapon.  

Now, I'm not going to jump on the 8K gaming cart just yet, but it's not an unreasonable idea. The cheapest Samsung 8K TV is 55" and costs $2600, that's half the price of Apple's ProDisplay  XDR with 50% more pixels.  Even 4K had to start somewhere, and with the HDMI 2.1 support on the RTX 3000 series it's ok to try out 8K, if only to see how far we need to go.  My guess is, that by the end of the decade, 8K gaming will be every day .. just like 4K gaming is for me right now.

Siege:

The average of the percentages 365% and 328% would be 346,5% (or 246,5% faster)

comments.text: Truth is, the gaming market is painting itself into a corner and this graphic card belongs firmly in that corner. Gaming, like most competitive sports, has become the domain of those who are young enough to have fantastic reflexes and have vast wads of time (and money) to devote to their favorite online games. This is, in effect, shutting out a fair percentage of the population and depriving the industry of audience (and therefore revenue). The essence of any good game is simplicity and addiction. The best games have psychological or story hooks that are irresistible and hook a large percentage of the computer-owning population.  Remember those simple car games of the 90's? Well now you need a direct drive powered steering wheel and a multi-monitor frame to be competitive - so kiss goodbye to thousands and thousands of dollar. We've also lost the notion of good single-person games - so much is now geared to online gaming. And unless you have, at least, a 144Hz monitor (uber low latency of course) with an equally competent internet connection, well sorry buddy, you're an also-ran. I can draw an analogy here. When I was young the craze was windsurfing. You stood on a board which floated even with you on it. Your sail had a few braces but was distinctly low tech. Nevertheless a tremendous amount of fun could be had for relatively few dollars. Plus those boards didn't demand a huge amount of skill to start having fun. Fast forward to today. If you don't have a high-tech "sinker" board and high-tech (but hard to properly use) sail, then you're nowhere. The cost has also sky-rocketed. In adjusted dollars my first setup cost $1000 and my current setup cost closer to $8000. Now go to your average lake or ocean. How many windsurfers do you see?
